To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the interface strength between graphite particles and ferrite is higher when graphite particles have a spiky shape, compared to when graphite particles have smooth morphology.
the strength of the graphite–ferritic matrix interface is higher for graphite–ferrites with a spiky morphology, compared to graphite–ferrities with a smooth morphology.

ferrite–graphitic interfaces with a spiky morphology exhibit a higher resistance to delamination, compared to ferrite–graphit interfaces with smooth morphology, due to the mechanical interlocking of graphite spikes and ferritic matrix.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the microstructure–mechanical properties relationship in the case of compacted graphite iron.
the characterization of the strength of the interface metal–graphite in CG iron, with the goal of developing a new heat treatment for CG iron to improve the mechanical properties of this material.
the characterization of the strength of the interface between graphite particles and metal matrix in CGI, and the influence of the heat-treatment on the mechanical properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the strength of the graphite–matrix interface in CG iron depends on the morphology of the graphite particles and the ferrite–cementite ratio of the matrix, and that the strength is not only related to the chemical composition and the mechanical properties of the matrix.
the interface strength is higher for ferrite–graphitic interfaces with spiky morphology than for interfaces with smooth morphology.
, after the heat treatment, the graphite particles are more strongly bonded with the matrix, resulting in a more compact graphite iron.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the graphite particles in compacted graphite iron are not necessarily weak spots in the material and, therefore, the mechanical properties can be further improved.
the graphite–matrix interfaces in compacted graphite iron can be improved by a heat-treatment that promotes the formation of graphite–ferritic interfaces with a spiky morphology.
the strength of the interface between the matrix and the graphite particles is an important property for the mechanical behavior of compacted graphite iron.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the graphite morphology is the key parameter in determining the metal–graphitic interface strength in compacted graphite iron.
a heat treatment at 700 ° C for 60 h is able to improve the mechanical properties of compacted graphite iron by strengthening the ferrite– graphite interface.
the annealing heat-treatment, applied to the as-cast cylinder head, increases the resistance of the metal–matrix interface to crack initiation.
